analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals buy 90-day supplies of prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Americans import prescription drugs from Canada never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the Health and Human Services Secretary, within 180 days, to write rules allowing individuals to buy prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies for personal use, up to a 90-day supply with a valid US prescription. Canadian pharmacies would have to be licensed, at least five years old, and meet federal safety and quality-testing criteria, and the FDA would publish a list of approved pharmacies. The bill excludes controlled substances, biologics, injectable and refrigerated drugs. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially those without insurance or with high cost-sharing, who could buy the same drugs from Canadian pharmacies where prices are often far lower. It helps only people with medications that qualify for importation, since it excludes biologics, injectables, controlled substances, and refrigerated drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying high US drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Requires the HHS Secretary to promulgate regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to import prescription drugs for personal use in up to 90-day supplies [S2]

Only allows drugs purchased from Canadian pharmacies the Secretary certifies as licensed and meeting quality-assurance, testing, and accountability criteria, and requires FDA to publish a list of approved pharmacies [S2]
Only permits drugs filled with a valid US physician prescription, with the same active ingredients, dosage form, and strength as FDA-approved drugs [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US revenue depends on keeping American prices above Canadian ones. If US prices fell toward Canadian levels, that revenue pressure would fall on the industry, though the narrow personal-importation scope limits the immediate effect.

drawbacks.text: The scope is narrow: it excludes biologics, biotech-manufactured drugs, injectables, IV drugs, refrigerated drugs, and controlled substances, so many expensive modern treatments, including most cancer and specialty drugs, would not qualify [S2]

Opponents of drug importation have long argued it creates safety risks from foreign supply chains; this bill addresses that with certification, quality testing, and an approved-pharmacy list, but oversight of thousands of individual shipments would still be harder than of the domestic supply chain [S2]
It does nothing to lower the underlying US price; patients without easy access to approved Canadian pharmacies would get no relief [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who can use it, the bill offers a direct way around US drug prices, with meaningful safety guardrails. The honest cost is that it is a workaround, not a fix: it leaves US prices untouched, excludes many of the most expensive drugs, and shifts verification burden onto a certification system the Secretary would have to build. A well-designed but limited policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the bill on July 31, 2024, with Grassley, Brown, King, Shaheen, Whitehouse, Baldwin, and Merkley as original cosponsors [S2]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on July 31, 2024 [S4]
No further action was taken; no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action is recorded before the 118th Congress ended [S4]
Seven senators cosponsored the bill, including one Republican (Grassley), five Democrats, and one Independent (King) [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who keep the US price structure intact and face no competition from Canadian pharmacies; patients continue paying US prices.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction, with a Republican (Grassley) and an Independent (King) among its seven cosponsors, but neither party's leadership brought it to a vote.

industries.note: Personal importation lets Americans buy the same drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into manufacturer revenue that depends on higher US prices. The industry has long opposed importation on safety grounds.
The bill would create a certified channel of American customers for Canadian pharmacies that meet federal criteria, aligning their business with patients seeking lower prices.
Some prescription volume could shift to Canadian pharmacies, but the narrow scope (90-day personal supplies, no biologics or controlled substances) limits the lost business.
